title: Quantitative cross-linking via engineered cysteines to study inter-domain interactions in bacterial collagenases
author: Serwanja, Brandstetter, et al.

steps.title: Design cross‑linked protein variants
steps.instruction: Plan the cysteine pair to introduce by (1) performing a multiple‑sequence alignment of the target protein with homologues to locate conserved residues, (2) avoiding mutation of conserved amino acids, (3) mutating any naturally occurring non‑conserved cysteines, and (4) using PyMol or UCSF Chimera to model the desired domain orientation, selecting surface‑accessible side‑chains with Cβ–Cβ distance < 5 Å for cysteine substitution (yielding an S–S distance ≈ 2 Å) or, if unavailable, choosing more distant pairs for use with bridging cross‑linkers.

substeps.instruction: Perform multiple‑sequence alignment of target protein with known homologues.
Do not target conserved residues for mutation.
Mutate any non‑conserved native cysteines to other residues.
Visualize the target conformation in PyMol or UCSF Chimera:
• Load crystal structures, homology models, or AlphaFold models.
• Model the two domains in the desired relative orientation.

• Identify surface‑accessible side‑chains facing each other with Cβ–Cβ distance < 5 Å and mutate them to cysteines (S–S distance ≈ 2 Å). If no suitable pair exists, consider more distant residues together with a bridging cross‑linker.

steps.title: Pack and equilibrate ATS column
steps.instruction: Pack a 50 mL gravity‑flow column (or columns) with 10 mL Activated Thiol Sepharose 4B resin and equilibrate the column(s) with 100 mL oxidation buffer.

steps.title: Load protein onto ATS column
steps.instruction: Load 40 mL of concentrated, clarified protein onto the equilibrated ATS column(s).

steps.title: Incubate column overnight
steps.instruction: Place the column(s) on a horizontal tube‑roller mixer at 4 °C and incubate overnight to allow binding of any thiol‑containing molecules to the matrix.

steps.title: Collect flow‑through and wash
steps.instruction: After the overnight incubation, collect the flow‑through (which contains cross‑linked protein) by gravity flow and store it on ice; then wash the column with 50 mL oxidation buffer and take a 20 µL SDS‑PAGE sample of both the flow‑through and the wash.

steps.title: Elute bound protein with β‑ME
steps.instruction: Elute any matrix‑bound protein by loading 40 mL oxidation buffer containing 20 mM β‑mercaptoethanol, incubating on the tube‑roller mixer at room temperature for 5 min, then collecting the eluate by gravity flow; prepare a 20 µL SDS‑PAGE sample of the eluate to monitor non‑cross‑linked protein.

steps.title: Wash and regenerate ATS column
steps.instruction: Wash the ATS column sequentially with 250 mL 0.1 % v/v Triton™ X‑100 (gravity flow), then 500 mL water to remove residual detergent, and finally regenerate the column with 15 mL of 1.5 mM 2,2′‑dipyridyl disulfide (pH 8.0) and store at 4 °C.

steps.title: Analyze ATS fractions by SDS‑PAGE
steps.instruction: Analyze all ATS fractions (flow‑through, wash, and eluate) using 12 % SDS‑PAGE stained with Coomassie‑R250 to assess cross‑linking efficiency.

steps.title: Perform size‑exclusion chromatography
steps.instruction: Carry out SEC at 4 °C using a Superdex 200 10/300 GL column pre‑equilibrated with filtered, degassed size‑exclusion buffer that contains no β‑ME.

steps.title: Concentrate and clarify ATS flow‑through
steps.instruction: Concentrate the ATS flow‑through with an Amicon Ultra‑15 device (10 000 MWCO) at 4 000 × g, 4 °C for 10 min, then clarify the concentrate by centrifugation at 13 000 g, 4 °C for 30 min.

steps.title: Load and run SEC column
steps.instruction: Load up to 10 mg of the clarified protein onto the SEC column and collect all elution fractions; take a 20 µL SDS‑PAGE sample from each fraction.

steps.title: Analyze SEC fractions by SDS‑PAGE
steps.instruction: Analyze the SEC fractions using 12 % SDS‑PAGE stained with Coomassie‑R250 to identify pure monomeric protein.

steps.title: Concentrate pure monomeric protein
steps.instruction: Pool the pure monomeric SEC fractions and concentrate them with an Amicon Ultra‑15 device (10 000 MWCO) at 4 000 × g, 4 °C for 10 min to the desired final concentration.

steps.title: Aliquot and flash‑freeze for storage
steps.instruction: Aliquot the concentrated protein into PCR tubes, flash‑freeze with liquid nitrogen, and store long‑term at –80 °C.

description: Inter-domain movements act as important activity modulators in multi-domain proteins; whether it is by creating binding surfaces for ligands,2,3,4 or by enabling catalysis or receptor activation.3,5,6,7 To unravel their functional significance, it is crucial to be able to lock the target domains in distinct conformational states. This can be done by inter-domain cross-linking via engineered cysteine residues.8,9,10 This method has the advantage that the target protein can be reversibly maintained in a fixed conformational state. Upon addition of a reducing agent, the restraining linkage dissolves. Yet, this method entails pitfalls that need to be carefully handled, as one must avoid the presence of i) mislinked higher oligomeric species, and ii) a mixture of cross-linked and non-cross-linked proteins. Moreover, it is also vital that the engineered cysteine pair and the subsequently formed disulfide bond do not compromise the fold of the protein or annihilate critical functional residues or motifs. Here we describe the cross-linking of the collagenase unit (CU) of the collagenase ColG from Hathewaya histolytica. The CU is composed of the activator domain (AD) and peptidase domain (PD) and adopts an open conformation in the crystal structure. A two-state model of collagen degradation was proposed, in which the CU switches between an open and closed conformation.11 This protocol was established to generate cross-linked CU variants in different states of closure. Care was taken to address the aforementioned pitfalls, in order to produce pure, functional, homogenously cross-linked, monomeric protein.
